short: The revolt that cut the Tang empire in half and never let it recover.
full:
An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic parentage, held three frontier commands and perhaps 160,000 troops on the northeastern border. On 16 December 755 he marched south, took Luoyang within weeks and declared himself emperor of a new Yan dynasty. When the Tang court forced its generals to abandon the Tong Pass defences and fight in the open, the road to Chang'an lay open. Emperor Xuanzong fled towards Sichuan; at the Mawei post station his own escort mutinied and demanded the death of his consort Yang Guifei, and he gave her up.

An Lushan was murdered by his son in 757, who was in turn killed by another commander, and the revolt outlived all of them until 763. The Tang recovered its capitals only with Uyghur cavalry, paid for in silk and licensed looting. Registered population fell from about 53 million before the rising to under 17 million afterwards, a figure that measures the collapse of tax registration as much as death. The provincial commands that suppressed the rebellion were never disbanded.
